**Question 1:** Concerning His words, Exalted is He, ﴿As for him who gives and fears [God]﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said: it refers to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and this is also the view of the majority of the commentators (mufassirun). It is related from Amir ibn Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr that he said: Abu Bakr used to free elderly women and slave-women for the sake of Islam. His father, Quhafa, said to him: "My son, if you freed strong men who would protect you and stand with you?" He said: "O father, I only want what I want" [[Thus in the Kitab Asbab al-Nuzul and Ruh al-Ma'ani. In the copies of the original text: "ma yurid." In Tafsir al-Tha'labi and another narration in Asbab al-Nuzul: "If you were buying someone who would protect your back." He said: "I want the protection of my back."]].

It is related from Ibn Abbas regarding His words, Exalted is He, ﴿As for him who gives﴾: that is, spends (badhala). ﴿And fears [God]﴾: that is, [fears] the prohibitions of God which He forbade. ﴿And affirms the best﴾: that is, [affirms] the replacement from God, Exalted is He, for His giving.

﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾. In the Sahih of Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no day on which the servants rise in the morning except that two angels descend, and one of them says: 'O Allah, give the one who spends a replacement,' and the other says: 'O Allah, give the one who withholds destruction.'" It is also narrated from the hadith of Abu al-Darda': that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no day whose sun sets except that two angels are sent beside it, calling out, which all of God's creation hears except the two weighty ones [jinn and humankind]: 'O Allah, give the one who spends a replacement, and give the one who withholds destruction.'" Then Allah, Exalted is He, revealed in the Qur'an concerning that: ﴿As for him who gives…﴾ the verses.

The commentators (ahl al-tafsir) said: ﴿As for him who gives﴾ [means] to the needy. Qatadah said: [it means] he gave the right of God, Exalted is He, which was incumbent upon him. Al-Hasan said: he gave sincerity from his heart.

﴿And affirms the best﴾: that is, [affirms] "There is no god but Allah," as said by al-Dahhak, al-Sulami, and also Ibn Abbas. Mujahid said: [it means] Paradise, the evidence for which is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿For those who did good is the best [reward] and an increase﴾ [Yunus: 26] — the verse. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 92, verses 11–13:**

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And his wealth will not avail him when he falls [into destruction]﴾. That is, when he dies. It is said: "radiya al-rajulu yarda radan," meaning the man perished. The poet said:

*I turned desire away from them out of fear of destruction.*

Abu Salih and Zayd ibn Aslam said: "Idha taraddá" means he falls into Jahannam. From this comes "al-mutaraddiyah." It is also said: "radiya fi al-bi'r" and "taraddá," meaning he fell into a well, or plunged down from a mountain. It is said: "Ma adri ayna radiya?" meaning, "Where did he go?"

"Ma" may be a negation, meaning: his wealth will not avail him anything at all. It may also be an interrogative expressing reproach, meaning: what will his wealth avail him when he has perished and fallen into Jahannam?

That is, it is incumbent upon us to explain the path of guidance from the path of misguidance. "Al-huda" here means the clarification of the rulings. This was said by al-Zajjaj, meaning: upon Allah lies the clarification, the clarification of what He made lawful and unlawful, and of obedience and disobedience. This was said by Qatadah. Al-Farra' said: whoever follows the guidance, Allah's way is upon him, based on His saying: ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾ [al-Nahl: 9]. He says: whoever seeks Allah, he is upon the straight path.

It is also said: its meaning is that upon us lies the guidance and the misguidance, but He left out the misguidance, as in His saying: ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26], and ﴿In Whose hand is the dominion of everything﴾ [Ya-Sin: 83]. And as He said: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], while they also protect from the cold; this is also from al-Farra'.

It is also said: that is, upon us is the reward of the guidance which We have guided [people] to.

﴿And indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the first [life]﴾. "Al-akhirah" is Paradise, and "al-ula" is this world. Atta' narrated likewise from Ibn 'Abbas. That is, this world and the Hereafter belong to Allah, the Exalted. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the reward of this world and the Hereafter. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world, then with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Nisa': 134]. So whoever seeks both from other than their Owner has indeed erred from the way.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 92, verse 19–21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And no one has any favour with him that is repaid﴾, meaning: he does not give charity so as to be recompensed for a favour, but he seeks only the Face of his Lord, the Most High (al-A'la), i.e., the Exalted; ﴿and he will surely be pleased﴾, i.e., with the reward. 'Ata' and al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The polytheists tortured Bilal, while Bilal kept saying, "One, One." The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by him and said: [One (meaning God, exalted is He) will save you]. [Then he said to Abu Bakr: [O Abu Bakr, indeed Bilal is being tortured for the sake of God]. So Abu Bakr understood what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) intended, so he went back to his house, took a rithl of gold, and went with it to Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and said to him: "Will you sell me Bilal?" He said: "Yes." So he bought him and freed him. The polytheists said: "Abu Bakr only freed him because of a favour he had owed him," so this was revealed: ﴿And no one has any favour with him﴾, i.e., with Abu Bakr, of any favour, i.e., any hand or kindness, ﴿that is repaid﴾; rather [he does it] seeking the Face of his Lord, the Most High, for what he did. It was also said: Abu Bakr bought Bilal from Umayyah and Ubayy ibn Khalaf for a cloak and ten awaq, and freed him for God's sake, so this was revealed: ﴿Indeed your striving is diverse﴾ [al-Layl: 4]. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: It reached me that Umayyah ibn Khalaf said to Abu Bakr, when Abu Bakr said to him: "Will you sell him to me?": "Yes, I will sell him for Nistas." Nistas was a slave of Abu Bakr, the owner of ten thousand dinars, servants, maidservants and livestock, and he was a polytheist. Abu Bakr urged him to Islam, on condition that he keep his wealth, but he refused, so Abu Bakr sold him in exchange for him. The polytheists said: "Abu Bakr did not do this to Bilal except because of a favour Bilal had done for him," so this was revealed: ﴿And no one has any favour with him that is repaid.﴾ ﴿Except⦆ seeking, i.e., but rather seeking. It is an exceptive construction that is disjunct (munqati'), and therefore it is in the accusative (nusibat). Like your saying: "There is no one in the house except a donkey." The nominative is also permissible. Yahya ibn Wathhab recited (إِلَّا ابْتِغَاءُ وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ) with the nominative, according to the dialect of those who say that the nominative is permissible in the excepted term. He also cited in both dialects the verse of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim:

Its abodes have become desolate wastes with no companion in them,
except the gazelle-calves and the ostriches moving about.

And the saying of another:

A land in which there is no companion,
except the young gazelles and except the camels.

And in the Revelation: ﴿They would not have done it except for a few of them﴾ [al-Nisa': 66], and this has already been mentioned.

(Seeking the Face of his Lord, the Most High): i.e., His good pleasure and that which brings one close to Him. "The Most High" is an attribute of the Lord who deserves the attributes of exaltedness. It is also permissible that "seeking the Face of his Lord" be an object of purpose in meaning, because the meaning of the statement is: He gives his wealth only seeking the Face of his Lord, not to repay His favour.

(And he will surely be pleased): i.e., He will give him in Paradise what pleases him, and that is that He will give him multiples of what he spent. Abu Hayyan al-Taymi related from his father, from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: [May God have mercy on Abu Bakr! He married me to his daughter, carried me to the abode of emigration, and freed Bilal from his own wealth]. When Abu Bakr bought him, Bilal said to him: "Did you buy me for your work or for the work of God?" He said: "Rather for the work of God." He said: "Then leave me and the work of God," so he freed him. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, used to say: "Abu Bakr is our master, and he freed our master" (meaning Bilal, may God be pleased with him). 'Ata' said, and he related from Ibn 'Abbas: The surah was revealed concerning Abu al-Dahdah, regarding the palm tree which he bought for a garden of his, as mentioned by al-Tha'labi from 'Ata'. Al-Qushayri said from Ibn 'Abbas: for forty palm trees, and he did not name the man. 'Ata' said: A man of the Ansar had a palm tree whose dates fell into the house of a neighbour of his, and his children would take them, so he complained of that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: [Will you sell it for a palm tree in Paradise?] He refused, and went out, and Abu al-Dahdah met him and said: "Would you like to sell it to me for (al-Husna): a garden of his?" He said: "It is yours." Abu al-Dahdah came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, buy it from me for a palm tree in Paradise." He said: [Yes, by Him in whose hand is my soul]. He said: "It is yours, O Messenger of God." The Prophet (ﷺ) called the Ansari neighbour and said: [Take it]. Then was revealed: ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ [al-Layl: 1] to the end of the surah, concerning the garden of Abu al-Dahdah and the owner of the palm tree. ﴿As for he who gives and fears God﴾ refers to Abu al-Dahdah; ﴿and believes in the best﴾, i.e., in the reward; ﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾, meaning Paradise. ﴿But as for he who is miserly and considers himself free of need﴾ refers to the Ansari; ﴿and denies the best﴾, i.e., the reward; ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾, meaning Hell. ﴿And his wealth will not avail him when he falls [into destruction]⦆, i.e., dies. Up to His saying: ﴿None will burn therein except the most wretched﴾, referring by this to the Khazraji, who was a hypocrite and died in his hypocrisy. ﴿But the most righteous will be spared from it﴾ refers to Abu al-Dahdah, ﴿who gives his wealth to purify himself﴾, in the price of that palm tree. ﴿And no one has any favour with him that is repaid﴾, i.e., who would reward him for it, referring to Abu al-Dahdah. ﴿And he will surely be pleased﴾, when God admits him to Paradise. The more widespread view is that the surah was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, and this is related from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and others. We have already mentioned another report about Abu al-Dahdah in Surat al-Baqarah, at His saying: ﴿Who is it that would lend to God a goodly loan﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245]. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

except the young gazelles and except the camels.

And in the Revelation: ﴿They would not have done it except for a few of them﴾ [al-Nisa': 66], and this has already been mentioned.

(Seeking the Face of his Lord, the Most High): i.e., His good pleasure and that which brings one close to Him. "The Most High" is an attribute of the Lord who deserves the attributes of exaltedness. It is also permissible that "seeking the Face of his Lord" be an object of purpose in meaning, because the meaning of the statement is: He gives his wealth only seeking the Face of his Lord, not to repay His favour.

(And he will surely be pleased): i.e., He will give him in Paradise what pleases him, and that is that He will give him multiples of what he spent. Abu Hayyan al-Taymi related from his father, from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: [May God have mercy on Abu Bakr! He married me to his daughter, carried me to the abode of emigration, and freed Bilal from his own wealth]. When Abu Bakr bought him, Bilal said to him: "Did you buy me for your work or for the work of God?" He said: "Rather for the work of God." He said: "Then leave me and the work of God," so he freed him. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, used to say: "Abu Bakr is our master, and he freed our master" (meaning Bilal, may God be pleased with him). 'Ata' said, and he related from Ibn 'Abbas: The surah was revealed concerning Abu al-Dahdah, regarding the palm tree which he bought for a garden of his, as mentioned by al-Tha'labi from 'Ata'. Al-Qushayri said from Ibn 'Abbas: for forty palm trees, and he did not name the man. 'Ata' said: A man of the Ansar had a palm tree whose dates fell into the house of a neighbour of his, and his children would take them, so he complained of that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: [Will you sell it for a palm tree in Paradise?] He refused, and went out, and Abu al-Dahdah met him and said: "Would you like to sell it to me for (al-Husna): a garden of his?" He said: "It is yours." Abu al-Dahdah came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, buy it from me for a palm tree in Paradise." He said: [Yes, by Him in whose hand is my soul]. He said: "It is yours, O Messenger of God." The Prophet (ﷺ) called the Ansari neighbour and said: [Take it]. Then was revealed: ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ [al-Layl: 1] to the end of the surah, concerning the garden of Abu al-Dahdah and the owner of the palm tree. ﴿As for he who gives and fears God﴾ refers to Abu al-Dahdah; ﴿and believes in the best﴾, i.e., in the reward; ﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾, meaning Paradise. ﴿But as for he who is miserly and considers himself free of need﴾ refers to the Ansari; ﴿and denies the best﴾, i.e., the reward; ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾, meaning Hell. ﴿And his wealth will not avail him when he falls [into destruction]⦆, i.e., dies. Up to His saying: ﴿None will burn therein except the most wretched﴾, referring by this to the Khazraji, who was a hypocrite and died in his hypocrisy. ﴿But the most righteous will be spared from it﴾ refers to Abu al-Dahdah, ﴿who gives his wealth to purify himself﴾, in the price of that palm tree. ﴿And no one has any favour with him that is repaid﴾, i.e., who would reward him for it, referring to Abu al-Dahdah. ﴿And he will surely be pleased﴾, when God admits him to Paradise. The more widespread view is that the surah was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, and this is related from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and others. We have already mentioned another report about Abu al-Dahdah in Surat al-Baqarah, at His saying: ﴿Who is it that would lend to God a goodly loan﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245]. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 92, verse 19–21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And no one has any favour with him that is repaid﴾, meaning: he does not give charity so as to be recompensed for a favour, but he seeks only the Face of his Lord, the Most High (al-A'la), i.e., the Exalted; ﴿and he will surely be pleased﴾, i.e., with the reward. 'Ata' and al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The polytheists tortured Bilal, while Bilal kept saying, "One, One." The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by him and said: [One (meaning God, exalted is He) will save you]. [Then he said to Abu Bakr: [O Abu Bakr, indeed Bilal is being tortured for the sake of God]. So Abu Bakr understood what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) intended, so he went back to his house, took a rithl of gold, and went with it to Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and said to him: "Will you sell me Bilal?" He said: "Yes." So he bought him and freed him. The polytheists said: "Abu Bakr only freed him because of a favour he had owed him," so this was revealed: ﴿And no one has any favour with him﴾, i.e., with Abu Bakr, of any favour, i.e., any hand or kindness, ﴿that is repaid﴾; rather [he does it] seeking the Face of his Lord, the Most High, for what he did. It was also said: Abu Bakr bought Bilal from Umayyah and Ubayy ibn Khalaf for a cloak and ten awaq, and freed him for God's sake, so this was revealed: ﴿Indeed your striving is diverse﴾ [al-Layl: 4]. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: It reached me that Umayyah ibn Khalaf said to Abu Bakr, when Abu Bakr said to him: "Will you sell him to me?": "Yes, I will sell him for Nistas." Nistas was a slave of Abu Bakr, the owner of ten thousand dinars, servants, maidservants and livestock, and he was a polytheist. Abu Bakr urged him to Islam, on condition that he keep his wealth, but he refused, so Abu Bakr sold him in exchange for him. The polytheists said: "Abu Bakr did not do this to Bilal except because of a favour Bilal had done for him," so this was revealed: ﴿And no one has any favour with him that is repaid.﴾ ﴿Except⦆ seeking, i.e., but rather seeking. It is an exceptive construction that is disjunct (munqati'), and therefore it is in the accusative (nusibat). Like your saying: "There is no one in the house except a donkey." The nominative is also permissible. Yahya ibn Wathhab recited (إِلَّا ابْتِغَاءُ وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ) with the nominative, according to the dialect of those who say that the nominative is permissible in the excepted term. He also cited in both dialects the verse of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim:

Its abodes have become desolate wastes with no companion in them,
except the gazelle-calves and the ostriches moving about.
